Question: I am the power of attorney, but my parents’ house is in a reversed mortgage and they have both passed away. Can I keep the house?
Answer: If you can pay for it you can buy the house from the estate. Your Power of Attorney ended when the Maker(s) died. It’s of zero use now. All that matters now is who is the Executor of the Estate? Because THAT is who will decide what happens to the house. The reverse mortgage is now due in full - principal, accrued interest, and any other fees required. The estate will be given a short amount of time to pay the mortgage IN FULL. If you want to keep the house AND the Executor agrees, you will have to buy it from the estate. If you don’t have the cash or can’t get financed, the Executor of the estate will have to sell the property to pay the loan.

Question: Would you continue to have children if your first had a disability? Why or why not?
Answer: That’s a very good question, and certainly something that I imagine most parents think about. And every set of parents (or single parents, for that matter) can only answer this for themselves and their specific circumstances. When I was pregnant the first time, my husband and I discussed this at great length. Because we were older (I was 37 when I got pregnant the first time), the risk of a disability was higher than if we’d been 20 years younger. We would have terminated a pregnancy that was identified in the womb as having a serious defect. We were not in any position, financially or emotionally, to deal with a special needs child that had a serious disability. But not every disability can be identified before birth, and not every disability happens before birth. Things can happen during the delivery, or just not manifest themselves until after birth. And then there’s the consideration of whether the disability is genetic - meaning it could happen to more than one child born to a specific pair of people. We knew that having a severely disabled child would be a huge strain on us. And we decided then, while I was still pregnant with #1, that in any case we would not have another child, not just if the disability was genetic. We figured that in OUR specific circumstances, it wouldn’t be fair to a second child because the first would always HAVE to be a priority. Everything - money, time, emotion - would HAVE to go first to the disabled child, and the second child would be stuck with whatever could be spared. That’s no way for any child to grow up. Always feeling like they’re not important enough to deserve a priority spot.

Question: A homeless woman moved into a vacant house that is on land my job owns. Is she squatting or trespassing?

Question: Who attends a home inspection?
Answer: That’s up to the parties involved, and the showing restrictions for the property. Here, the buyer usually pays for the inspection. Anyone CAN attend the inspection, but there’s really little reason for anyone except one or both of the agents to do so. The homeowner may want to attend, if his agent cannot, but there’s really no reason for it. The only person who MUST be there is the inspector, although if the property is occupied, someone has to let him in. If it’s vacant, the inspector may have access to the an electronic lock box either with MLS credentials or a one-day code. Or, the Seller may authorize a mechanical lock box be used for contractors, inspectors, etc. If we represent the Buyer, who pays for the inspection, the boss normally goes along so she can get a heads up on anything he finds wrong. She’ll make a list of “must do NOW” items and let the Seller’s agent know, because those are things that will have to be fixed regardless of whether this transaction goes through or not. She considers it a professional courtesy to the other agent and the Seller. By getting a heads up, the Seller has time to get bids and not just accept the first one that comes in. We’re representing a seller right now whose tenant hasn’t finished vacating the property. So the showings and inspections require the boss to be present. And she does the same thing - gets a “must do NOW’ list from the inspector. We’re doing this right now - we have two things that the Seller MUST fix, even though the buyer has already cancelled the transaction. Question: Both the landlord and tenant passed away. The tenant was my boyfriend. What do I do?

In my US state, if the lease was only in your boyfriend’s name, then the contract ended when he died. You will have at least until the end of the month in which he died, assuming he had paid the rent, before you need to vacate. If you were living there with the landlord’s permission, then you are an “other occupant”. That only gives you the right to occupy the premises during the valid lease period, which ended when your boyfriend died. You CAN wait to be contacted by the new owner and request to rent by yourself, assuming you qualify and assuming you can afford whatever new price the landlord will be charging. But do yourself a favor and assume you will need to move ASAP. Get your plans made so you’re not trying to do it on short notice.

You SHOULD insist that your boyfriend have you added to the lease, at least as an “other occupant”. That gives you the legal right to occupy the premises as long as the lease exists. As an “other occupant”, you have no financial liability for the rent but also no rights to occupy the premises if your boyfriend dies, moves, or otherwise terminates the lease. As a “co-tenant”, you are a tenant yourself, and therefore can occupy the premises as long as the lease is valid (and you comply with the lease requirements, of course, including paying the rent) regardless of what your boyfriend does.

Question: What happens to a dead corpse when there are no family members to sign a mandatory form for cremation and the funeral home refuses to do a cremation until legal forms are signed?

Property taxes paid to the city/county include an allocation for the “Indigent Fund” (name varies by jurisdiction). That fund is used for numerous things, including disposition of unclaimed bodies. Each participating funeral home in the city/county goes on the roster for being assigned pick ups for bodies. In my county, they rotate monthly, just like the towing companies. The funeral home will perform whichever disposition is called for in the contract - burial or cremation. The funeral home will prep the body for burial in a cheap particleboard box, or have the cremains put into a cheap plastic container. The deceased will then be handed off to cemetery workers - every city/county has a “Potters Field” where indigents are buried. The worker(s) dig(s) a hole, inserts the remains, and that’s that. There’s no headstone - only a numbered marker that corresponds to a record in the cemetery’s office.

Question: What happens to a defendant if they are deemed incompetent for trial?
Answer: Laws vary by jurisdiction. As this is an international site, the laws vary WIDELY. In the US, a defendant in a criminal trial must be competent to aid in his own defense. If his attorney can convince a judge he is not, the defendant will be held and treated in a secure psychiatric facility until he IS deemed competent to stand trial. Keep in mind that being competent to stand trial and pleading “not guilty by reason of insanity” are two entirely different things. To be competent to stand trial, the defendant must be capable of understanding what is going on, to communicate with his defense team, and to make decisions about his defense. There is no time limit to how long he can be held in the facility. The Statute of Limitations for his crime is suspended beginning on the date he is deemed “restored to competency”. If, after treatment, the defendant is deemed “unable to ever be restored to competency”, the charges will be withdrawn without prejudice (which means they CAN be re-filed, should he ever magically become competent). He will then undergo involuntary commitment proceedings so he will be institutionalized for the safety of the community.

Question: How do I sell my house with him living here and he expects a lot of money? I own the house solely.

Every jurisdiction has different timelines for this - in my state, the termination notice must be served 30 days before the first day of the month in which the tenancy will end. So to get someone out by the end of September, he’d have to be served by August 1. If he refuses to vacate, then you follow your jurisdiction’s procedures and evict him. Then law enforcement officers will remove him for you. Just be aware that he will likely trash the place, so you won’t be able to sell it until you’ve repaired all the damages, or you’ll have to discount the list price to account for the needed repairs.
